title: Squarespace vs Shopify: Which One Is Right for a Small Shop?
excerpt: Squarespace vs Shopify for a small shop: 2026 prices and fees side by side, what each one is good at, and how to choose without overpaying.
seoTitle: Squarespace vs Shopify: Which Is Right for a Small Shop?
seoDescription: Squarespace vs Shopify for a small shop: 2026 prices and fees side by side, what each one is good at, and how to choose without overpaying.
imageAlt: Squarespace vs Shopify: the cheapest plan, the extra fee on sales and the card rate for each
body:
Note: Prices are for the US and were last checked on November 25, 2026. Both companies change their pricing, so check Squarespace's pricing page and Shopify's pricing page before you decide.

I build websites on both Squarespace and Shopify, so I don't have a favorite to sell you. They're both good. They're just good at different things.

My short answer: if your business is mostly a store, and you plan to grow it into a big one, go with Shopify. If you need a good-looking website that also sells a handful of products or services, Squarespace is usually simpler and cheaper. The rest of this post is the longer answer.

Squarespace vs Shopify at a glance

SquarespaceShopify
Best forA website that also sellsA store first
Cheapest plan that can sellBasic: $19 a monthBasic: $29 a month
Extra fee on sales2% on Basic, none on Core and upNone with Shopify Payments
Card rate on that plan2.9% + 30¢2.9% + 30¢
Add-onsA small set of extensions, plus plugins you add with codeA large app store
Free trial14 days3 days, then $1 a month for 3 months

Monthly prices are what you pay when you pay for the year up front.

Squarespace vs Shopify pricing

Here's what each plan costs a month, paid yearly and paid month to month.

Squarespace Basic$19$252.9% + 30¢, plus a 2% fee on sales
Squarespace Core$29$392.9% + 30¢
Squarespace Plus$49$652.7% + 30¢
Squarespace Advanced$99$1392.5% + 30¢
Shopify Basic$29$392.9% + 30¢
Shopify Grow$79$1052.7% + 30¢
Shopify Advanced$299$3992.5% + 30¢

Two things stand out to me.

First, the fair comparison for a small shop is Squarespace Core against Shopify Basic. They cost the same, $29 a month paid yearly, and neither one adds an extra fee on your sales. Squarespace's $19 Basic plan looks cheaper, but its 2% fee on every sale costs more than the $10 difference once you sell over $500 a month.

Second, the plans pull apart as you move up. Squarespace's top plan is $99 a month. Shopify's third plan is $299. If you only want lower card rates, Squarespace gets you there for a lot less.

One Shopify fee to know about: if you use a payment provider other than Shopify Payments, Shopify adds its own fee on each sale. It's 2% on Basic, 1% on Grow and 0.6% on Advanced.

I go through every Squarespace plan in more detail in my Squarespace pricing post.

Is Squarespace good for ecommerce?

Yes, for a small shop. Every Squarespace plan can sell an unlimited number of products, and the tools most small shops need are built in: shipping rates, sales tax, discounts, gift cards, customer reviews and point of sale.

Where Squarespace is strongest is everything around the store. Your homepage, your About page, your blog and your products all live in one place and look like they belong together. If your site has to do more than sell, that matters a lot.

Its limits show up when a store gets complicated. A product can have up to 250 variants, and there's no big app store to fill the gaps.

Where Shopify is the better choice

Shopify is built to be a store first, and it shows. I'd pick it when:

  • You have a big catalog. Hundreds or thousands of products are easier to manage in Shopify.

  • You need something specific. Shopify's app store has an app for almost anything, like wholesale pricing or a loyalty program.

  • The store is the whole business. If you're planning to grow fast and sell in a lot of places, you'll be glad you started there.

The trade-off is that apps add up. Many of them have their own monthly fee, so the real cost of a Shopify store is usually the plan plus a few apps.

What about personalized products?

This is the one place I see people move to Shopify when they didn't need to.

Say you sell jewelry and want to charge $12 for engraving. Squarespace can't add a price to an option on its own, so the usual advice is "switch to Shopify," where an options app does it for about $9 to $20 a month. That works, but it also means rebuilding your whole site on a new platform to solve one problem.

I built OptionKit for this. It adds options with prices to a Squarespace product page, like a paid checkbox, text priced by the letter, or a file upload. It's $12 a month per store, with no fee per order, and it needs Squarespace's Core plan or higher. I'm biased, so here's a fuller comparison that tries to be fair to both sides: Squarespace vs Shopify for personalized products.

If you sell handmade products and you're also thinking about a marketplace, I wrote a separate comparison of Squarespace vs Etsy.

Can you switch later?

You can, but it's a rebuild, not a move. Products and customers can be exported from one and imported into the other. Your design can't. Pages, layouts and blog styling all get made again on the new platform.

That's why I'd rather help someone pick the right one up front. If you're stuck between the two, book a free consultation and I'll tell you which one I'd choose for your shop.

Frequently asked questions

Is Squarespace cheaper than Shopify?

At the low end they cost about the same. Squarespace Core and Shopify Basic are both $29 a month when you pay yearly, and neither one adds a fee on your sales. Higher up, Squarespace costs less: its top plan is $99 a month, and Shopify's Advanced plan is $299.

Does Squarespace charge transaction fees?

Only on the Basic plan, which adds 2% to each sale. Core, Plus and Advanced have no transaction fee. You still pay card processing on every plan, starting at 2.9% + 30¢.

Is Shopify or Squarespace better for a small business?

If your website needs to do more than sell, like show your work or run a blog, Squarespace is usually the better fit. If the store is the whole business and you expect a big catalog, Shopify is.

Can you use Shopify with Squarespace?

Yes. Shopify has a Buy Button you can paste into a Squarespace page. It means paying for two systems, and the checkout is run by Shopify, so it's usually more than a small shop needs.

Conclusion

For a small shop, I don't think there's a wrong answer here, just a better fit. Pick Squarespace if you want one good-looking site that also sells. Pick Shopify if the store is the business and you expect it to get big. And if the only thing pushing you toward Shopify is product options, try adding them to Squarespace first.

title: How to Sell Gift Cards on Squarespace
excerpt: How Squarespace gift cards work, how to set one up step by step, what your customer sees at checkout, and the limits to know before the holidays.
seoTitle: Squarespace Gift Cards: How to Set Up and Sell Them
seoDescription: How Squarespace gift cards work, how to set one up step by step, what your customer sees at checkout, and the limits to know before the holidays.
imageAlt: A Squarespace gift card product with an amount dropdown and a Purchase button
body:
Gift cards are one of the easiest things to add to a Squarespace store. They're included on every plan, and there isn't much to set up.

Here's how Squarespace gift cards work, how to set one up, and a few limits worth knowing before you start selling them.

How do gift cards work on Squarespace?

A gift card is its own kind of product. When someone buys one, Squarespace emails a code to the person they're buying it for, or to the buyer if they'd rather print it or pass it along themselves.

The person with the code types it in at checkout, and the value comes off their order total. That includes tax and shipping. If the order costs more than the gift card, they pay the rest with a card. If it costs less, the balance stays on the gift card for next time.

Squarespace gift cards never expire.

What you need before you start

  • A plan that can sell. All four current plans (Basic, Core, Plus and Advanced) include gift cards.

  • A way to get paid. Connect Squarespace Payments, Stripe or PayPal.

  • A store page. That's where the gift card will show up.

  • Sales tax set up, if you collect it. Buying a gift card isn't taxed, but the orders people place with one are. Here's how to set up sales tax on Squarespace.

  • The right currency. Check your store's currency first. Once you sell a gift card, even in a test order, you can't change it.

How to set up gift cards on Squarespace

  1. Add a new product to your store and select Gift Card.

  2. Give it a name and a short description. The name only shows on the product page, not in the gift card email.

  3. Add an image. A simple graphic with your logo works well.

  4. Set the amounts. Squarespace starts you with four. Click the Amount field to change them, or click Add for more.

  5. Hover over Save and click Publish.

If you're not ready to sell it yet, click Save instead and it stays hidden. You can also schedule it to go live on a certain day.

What your customer sees

Your customer picks an amount from a dropdown and clicks Purchase. That takes them straight to checkout, where they choose one of two delivery options:

  • Email to Recipient. They enter the recipient's name and email, a short message (up to 80 characters) and their own name. The gift card goes straight to the recipient.

  • Email to You. The gift card comes to the buyer, who can print it or forward it later.

The email goes out as soon as the purchase goes through. If a customer wants it to arrive on a birthday or a holiday, they should pick Email to You and forward it that day.

Squarespace gift card limits to know about

  • They're digital only. Squarespace doesn't make or ship plastic gift cards. Customers can print the email.

  • Customers can't type in their own amount. They choose from the amounts you set, so give them a good range.

  • A gift card is bought on its own. It can't go in the cart with other products, and it's one gift card per order.

  • Discounts don't apply to buying one. A sale price or discount code won't take money off a gift card. They do still work on an order paid for with a gift card.

  • They don't work on subscriptions. Gift cards can pay for physical products, downloads and services, but not subscription products. They also can't be used for Acuity appointments.

  • Only unused gift cards can be refunded. Once part of the balance has been spent, you can't refund it.

  • In person takes an extra step. You can't take a gift card through Squarespace's point of sale, but you can redeem one in the Squarespace app on an iPhone.

How to check a Squarespace gift card balance

Your customer can see the balance in the email they got, and again any time they enter the code at checkout.

To see every gift card you've sold, open Products & Services, click Orders, then View gift cards. You'll see who each one went to, what it started at and what's left. If a customer loses their code, you can resend the gift card email from the order.

What about gift wrap and gift messages?

Gift cards are for the shopper who doesn't know what to buy. A lot of holiday orders are the other kind: someone buying one of your products as a gift.

For those orders, Squarespace lets you add a gift message box at checkout with a custom checkout form. What it can't do on its own is charge for an extra, like $5 for gift wrap.

That's one of the reasons I built OptionKit, a plugin that adds paid options to Squarespace product pages. A customer checks a box for gift wrap, the price is added to their total, and it all goes through your normal checkout. It's installed with Code Injection, so it needs the Core plan or higher. Here's how to add a gift wrap option to a Squarespace product.

Frequently asked questions

Do Squarespace gift cards expire?

No. Squarespace gift cards never expire, and you can't set an expiration date.

Can I sell physical gift cards on Squarespace?

No. Squarespace gift cards are digital codes sent by email. Customers can print the email, but Squarespace doesn't make or ship plastic cards.

Which Squarespace plans have gift cards?

All four current plans do: Basic, Core, Plus and Advanced.

Can a customer use a gift card and a credit card on the same order?

Yes. If the order costs more than the gift card, they pay the rest with a card. They can also use more than one gift card on the same order.

Is sales tax charged on a gift card?

Not when someone buys it. Tax is charged later, on the order the gift card is used for.

Conclusion

Gift cards on Squarespace are simple to set up, and that's most of the appeal. Check your currency, add the product, pick a few amounts and publish it. If you want them selling for the holidays, add a link to the gift card in your menu or on your homepage so people can find it.

title: Squarespace Code Injection: Where It Is and Which Plans Have It
excerpt: Where to find Code Injection in Squarespace 7.1, which plans have it, Header vs Footer, adding code to one page, and how to keep it from breaking your site.
seoTitle: Squarespace Code Injection: Where It Is and Which Plans Have It
seoDescription: Where to find Code Injection in Squarespace 7.1, which plans have it, Header vs Footer, adding code to one page, and how to keep it from breaking your site.
imageAlt: The Squarespace Code Injection panel, with a Header box and a Footer box
body:
If you've ever followed a tutorial that says "just paste this into Code Injection," then spent ten minutes hunting for it, you're not alone. Squarespace has moved it more than once, and half the guides online still point to the old spot.

Here's where it is today, which plans have it, and how to use it without breaking your site.

What is Code Injection?

Code Injection is a set of boxes where you can paste a small piece of code that runs on your site. It's how you add things Squarespace doesn't do on its own, like a chat bubble, Google Tag Manager, a Pinterest tag, or a plugin like OptionKit.

You don't need to know how to code to use it. Most of the time, you're copying a line from the tool you're adding and pasting it into one box.

Where to find it in Squarespace 7.1

  1. Open your site and select Pages.

  2. Scroll to the bottom of the Pages panel.

  3. Select Custom Code, then Code Injection.

You'll see a Header box and a Footer box, plus a few others for special pages. Paste your code, then select Save.

If it isn't there, don't panic. Squarespace moves things around every so often. Search "Code Injection" in Squarespace's own help center and it'll show you where it is now.

Which Squarespace plans have Code Injection?

This is the part that trips people up. Code Injection is only on these plans:

  • Core, Plus or Advanced

  • The older Business, Commerce Basic or Commerce Advanced plans, if you're grandfathered in

The Basic plan doesn't have it, and neither did the old Personal plan. If you're on Basic and you need it, you'll have to upgrade. I break down what each plan costs in my Squarespace pricing post.

Header or Footer: which box do I use?

Use whichever one the tool's instructions tell you to. If they don't say, here's my rule of thumb:

  • Header is for tracking tags, like Google Tag Manager or a Pinterest tag. They want to load first.

  • Footer is for anything that changes how your pages look or behave. It loads after the page, so it doesn't slow down what your visitors see first.

Can I add code to just one page?

Yes. Every page has its own Code Injection box. Open the page's settings, select Advanced, and you'll find it there.

One catch: code on one page only runs on that page. If a tool needs to work across your whole store, like on the cart page too, it has to go in the site-wide Footer instead.

Here's a mix-up I see a lot: someone adds a chat widget to their Contact page's Code Injection, then wonders why it doesn't show up anywhere else. It's working fine. It's just only on that one page.

How to keep Code Injection from breaking your site

  • Only paste code from people you trust. Code in this box runs on every page, so a bad snippet can do real damage.

  • Keep a copy of what's in there. Before you change anything, copy everything in the box into a note on your computer. If something goes wrong, you can paste it right back.

  • Add one thing at a time. Then check your site. If something looks off, you'll know exactly which piece caused it.

  • Clean up old code. If you stopped using a tool, take its code out. Leftover snippets slow your site down and can clash with new ones.

Why I care about this one

I built OptionKit, a plugin that adds personalized product options to Squarespace stores, like engraving, gift wrap and per-letter pricing. It's installed with one line in the Code Injection Footer, so I've walked a lot of store owners through this exact screen.

For years, clients kept asking me, "Can customers add engraving for $15?" and I kept having to tell them Squarespace couldn't really do that. So I built the thing I kept wishing existed. You can read the whole story in I Built a Squarespace Plugin: Meet OptionKit.

If you're setting up OptionKit, here's the step-by-step for adding it with Code Injection.

Conclusion

Code Injection sounds technical, but it's really just a box you paste into. Find it under Pages › Custom Code › Code Injection, make sure your plan has it, and keep a copy of what's in there before you change anything. That's 90% of it.
summary: Where to find Code Injection in Squarespace 7.1, which plans have it, Header vs Footer, adding code to one page, and how to keep it from breaking your site.

title: Squarespace Shipping Options, Explained
excerpt: Flat rate, weight-based or carrier-calculated? How each Squarespace shipping option works, how to set up shipping, and how to offer free shipping.
seoTitle: Squarespace Shipping: Options, Setup and Free Shipping
seoDescription: Flat rate, weight-based or carrier-calculated? How each Squarespace shipping option works, how to set up shipping, and how to offer free shipping.
imageAlt: The three ways to charge for shipping on Squarespace: flat rate, weight-based and carrier-calculated
body:
Shipping is the part of a Squarespace store that people put off, because it looks like a lot of decisions. It's really three ways to charge, plus a few extras you can add later.

Here's what each option does, which one fits which kind of shop, and how to set it up.

What shipping options does Squarespace have?

Squarespace has three ways to charge for shipping:

  • Flat rate. One price per order, per item, or both.

  • Weight-based. The price goes up with the total weight of the order.

  • Carrier-calculated. Squarespace pulls live rates from the carrier at checkout. In the US, that's USPS, UPS or FedEx.

You can also add local pickup and local delivery, and you can have as many options as you need. At checkout, customers see them listed from cheapest to most expensive, with the cheapest one already selected.

Flat rate shipping

Flat rate is the simplest one, and it's where I'd start. You set a fee per order, a fee per item, or both. With $5 per order and $1 per item, an order with two items ships for $7.

It works well when your products are all about the same size and weight, or when they're small and worth a lot, like jewelry.

Weight-based shipping

With weight-based shipping, you set up weight ranges and a price for each one. For example, up to 1 pound is $5 and 1 to 5 pounds is $9.

Two things to know:

  • Every product needs a weight, or this won't work. You add it in the product editor under Fulfillment.

  • Set a generous price on your heaviest range, so one large order doesn't cost you money to ship.

It's a good fit when your products are similar in size but very different in weight.

Carrier-calculated shipping

This one shows your customer what the carrier would charge for their exact order and address. It's the most accurate option, and the one with the most setup.

  • It's on the Core, Plus and Advanced plans, not Basic. Here's what each plan costs.

  • It only works for orders shipped within your own country.

  • Every product needs a weight and dimensions, and you add the box sizes you ship in.

  • You can add a markup to cover packaging and your time.

It's worth it when shipping is a big part of what your customer pays, like with heavy or bulky products.

How to set up shipping on Squarespace

  1. Open the Shipping panel. It's under Settings, or you can press / and search for "Shipping."

  2. Click Add Shipping Option.

  3. Choose Flat Rate, Weight-based or Carrier-calculated.

  4. Give it a name your customers will understand, like "Standard shipping (3 to 5 days)," and enter your rates.

  5. For flat rate and weight-based options, choose where the option applies. You can pick countries, states or ZIP codes.

  6. Save, then place a test order to see what your customer sees.

If you sell physical products, you need at least one shipping, pickup or delivery option. Without one, customers can't check out.

How to offer free shipping on Squarespace

There are two ways to do it:

  • A free shipping option. Add a flat rate option and leave the fees at $0. Everyone gets it.

  • A free shipping discount. Use this when it comes with a condition, like free shipping on orders over $75. It can be a code customers type in, or on Core and higher plans it can apply on its own.

Local pickup and local delivery

If you have customers nearby, add a local pickup option so they can skip shipping. It's free to them. Keep in mind that customers can't choose a pickup time at checkout, so add your pickup hours and instructions to the pickup details. They show up in the customer's confirmation email.

Pickup orders can also be taxed differently from shipped ones. I cover that in my post on Squarespace sales tax.

Local delivery works by ZIP code. You list the ZIP codes you deliver to and, if you want, a delivery fee.

Why does checkout say shipping is unavailable?

If a customer sees a message that shipping isn't available for their address, it usually means none of your shipping options cover where they live. Check these first:

  • Your shipping zones. If an option is limited to certain countries, states or ZIP codes, everyone outside them is left out. To ship everywhere else, add an option set to Rest of the World.

  • Missing weights or dimensions. A carrier-calculated option won't show up if a product in the cart has no weight or dimensions, or if none of your boxes fit it.

  • Another country. Carrier-calculated rates don't cover orders going abroad. Add a flat rate or weight-based option for those.

What shipping settings can't do

Shipping options charge for getting the order to your customer. They can't charge for extras on one product, like rush processing or a gift box. Squarespace does have a handling fee, but it's a percentage of each item's price, added to the shipping cost of every order that uses that option.

For an extra the customer chooses, like "Rush: ships in 2 days, +$20," you need a product option with a price. I built a plugin called OptionKit that adds those to Squarespace. Here's my guide to adding product options in Squarespace, including what the built-in tools can do before you add anything.

Frequently asked questions

Does Squarespace offer free shipping?

Yes. You can add a flat rate option with the fees set to $0, or create a free shipping discount for orders over a certain amount.

Can I print shipping labels in Squarespace?

Yes, if you're in the US and on the Core plan or higher. You can buy and print UPS and USPS labels from your orders.

Can I charge different shipping for different products?

Yes. Fulfillment profiles let you limit a shipping option to certain products. A product can only be in one profile.

Which Squarespace plans have carrier-calculated shipping?

Core, Plus and Advanced. The Basic plan has flat rate and weight-based shipping.

Conclusion

Start with one flat rate option and a test order. That's enough to open your store. Once orders are coming in, you'll know whether you need weight ranges, live carrier rates or a free shipping offer, and you can add them one at a time.

title: A Custom Cake Order Form on Squarespace That Takes Payment
excerpt: Three ways to set up a custom cake order form on Squarespace, from a simple bakery order form to one where customers choose extras and pay up front.
seoTitle: Custom Cake Order Form on Squarespace (That Takes Payment)
seoDescription: Three ways to set up a custom cake order form on Squarespace, from a simple bakery order form to one where customers choose extras and pay up front.
imageAlt: A custom cake order form on a Squarespace product page, where the customer orders and pays on one page
body:
Most bakeries on Squarespace take custom cake orders the same way: a form on the website, then an email with a quote, then an invoice. It works, but every order takes a few emails before anyone pays.

There are three ways to set up a custom cake order form on Squarespace. I'll go from the simplest one to the one that takes payment up front, so you can pick what fits how you work.

What to ask on a cake order form

Whichever way you build it, the questions are about the same. Here's a cake order form template you can copy:

  • Date needed, and whether it's pickup or delivery

  • Size, or how many people it needs to serve

  • Cake flavor, filling and frosting

  • Message on the cake

  • Colors or theme, with a photo if they have one

  • Allergies or dietary needs

  • Name, phone and email

Keep it short. Every extra question is one more reason to give up halfway through.

Option 1: A form on a page

This is the classic bakery order form. Add a form block to a page, add the fields above, and Squarespace emails you each order. Form blocks have a file upload field, so customers can attach an inspiration photo.

A form collects the order, but not the money. You reply with a price and send an invoice, which you can do from Squarespace on any plan.

Good for: wedding cakes and anything fully custom, where you need to talk before you can give a price.

Option 2: A product with a form attached

If your cakes have set prices, sell them as products. Customers pay when they order, and there's no invoice to chase.

  1. Add the cake as a product in your store.

  2. Use variants for anything that changes the price, like size. Each variant can have its own price.

  3. In the product editor, go to Forms, click Add, then Create new form.

  4. Add your questions, like the message on the cake, the date and any allergies. Turn on Required for the ones you can't bake without.

The form pops up when the customer clicks Add to Cart, and their answers show up on the order and in your order email.

There are two limits. The form can't change the price, so you can't charge more for red velvet or a longer message unless you make each one a variant. And this kind of form doesn't have a file upload field.

Good for: a set cake menu with a few sizes and no paid extras.

Option 3: Options with prices on the cake's page

This is the one that works like a real order form and takes payment for everything at once. It's also the one that needs a plugin, because Squarespace can't put a price on an option by itself.

I built OptionKit for this. On the cake's own page, the customer picks everything and watches the total update:

  • Flavors, with a price on the ones that cost more, like red velvet for $5 extra

  • A message priced by the letter, with the first few letters free if you like

  • Extra candles, priced each

  • A photo upload for an edible photo topper

Then they pay in your normal Squarespace checkout, and the order shows the flavor and the message for your kitchen.

What it doesn't do: pickup dates and time slots aren't part of OptionKit. A short text field for the date works, or you can keep a simple form for the date alone.

OptionKit is $12 a month per store, and it's free to build and test on your squarespace.com address. It's installed with Code Injection, so it needs the Core plan or higher.

Good for: a cake menu where extras cost extra.

Photo uploadYesNoYes
Extra costNoneNone$12 a month

You don't have to pick just one. Products work well for the regular menu, and a form still makes sense for wedding cakes and anything unusual.

Pickup dates and how many cakes you can take

Two things trip bakeries up here.

First, Squarespace's local pickup option doesn't let customers choose a pickup time at checkout. Ask for the date in your form, and say on the product page how much notice you need.

Second, you probably can't make an unlimited number of cakes. Set the product's stock to what you can take on, and Squarespace will mark it sold out when you're full. Stock is one total, not a number per day, so update it as your calendar fills up.

Frequently asked questions

Can a Squarespace form take payment?

A form on a regular page collects the order but not the money. To take payment with the order, sell the cake as a product and attach a form to it, or add options with prices to the product page.

Can customers upload a photo with their cake order?

Yes, on a form block on a regular page. The form attached to a product doesn't have a file upload field, so for a product you'd need a plugin like OptionKit.

Can I charge by the letter for a message on a cake?

Not with Squarespace's built-in tools. OptionKit can price a message by the letter, with a number of free letters first.

Can customers choose a pickup date and time?

Not at checkout. Squarespace's local pickup doesn't let customers schedule a time, so ask for the date in your order form.

Conclusion

If every cake is a conversation, a form and an invoice is fine. If you have a menu, sell from it, and let customers pay when they order. You'll spend less time on email, and nobody has to wait on an invoice.

title: Squarespace vs Etsy for Handmade and Personalized Products
excerpt: Squarespace vs Etsy: what each one charges on a sale, where your shoppers come from, how personalized products work, and when to use both.
seoTitle: Squarespace vs Etsy for Handmade and Personalized Products
seoDescription: Squarespace vs Etsy: what each one charges on a sale, where your shoppers come from, how personalized products work, and when to use both.
imageAlt: Squarespace vs Etsy fees on one $50 sale in the US
body:
Note: Fees are for US sellers and were last checked on November 25, 2026. Etsy and Squarespace both change their fees, so check Etsy's fee policy and Squarespace's pricing page before you decide.

Squarespace and Etsy get compared a lot, but they aren't the same kind of thing. Etsy is a marketplace. Shoppers are already there, searching for things like yours. Squarespace is your own website. It's all yours, but you have to bring the shoppers.

That one difference explains almost everything else, including the fees. Here's how they compare if you sell handmade or personalized products.

Squarespace vs Etsy at a glance

SquarespaceEtsy
What it isYour own website and storeA shop inside a marketplace
Monthly costFrom $19 a month, paid yearlyNo monthly fee
Fees on each saleCard processing, from 2.9% + 30¢A listing fee, a transaction fee and payment processing
Where shoppers come fromYou bring themEtsy search, plus your own
Your own domain and designYesNo, it's a shop page on Etsy

What does Etsy charge?

Etsy doesn't have a monthly fee. It takes a cut of each sale instead:

  • Listing fee: $0.20 per listing. A listing lasts 4 months, then renews for another $0.20.

  • Transaction fee: 6.5% of the order total, including what you charge for shipping and gift wrap.

  • Payment processing: 3% + $0.25 in the US.

On a $50 sale, that comes to $5.20. Depending on where you are, Etsy may also charge a one-time set-up fee when you open your shop.

There's one more fee to know about, called Offsite Ads. Etsy advertises its sellers' listings around the web, and when one of those ads leads to a sale, Etsy takes 15% of that order. It drops to 12% once a shop has made $10,000 in a year. Smaller shops can opt out. Once a shop passes $10,000 in a year, it can't.

What does Squarespace charge?

Squarespace works the other way around. You pay for a plan, and the fees on each sale are small.

On the Core plan, which is $29 a month when you pay for the year, there's no listing fee and no transaction fee. You pay card processing of 2.9% + 30¢, so that same $50 sale costs you $1.75.

The cheaper Basic plan is $19 a month, but it adds a 2% fee on each sale. If you're selling regularly, Core is usually the better deal. I compare the plans in my Squarespace pricing post.

So which one is cheaper?

It depends on how much you sell. With $50 orders, Squarespace saves you about $3.45 on each sale, so the Core plan pays for itself at around nine sales a month. Below that, Etsy costs less. Above it, Squarespace does, and the gap keeps growing.

The fees aren't the whole picture, though. Etsy's cut is partly the price of being found. A new Squarespace site doesn't come with shoppers. You'll need to bring them in yourself, through Instagram, an email list, markets or search.

Selling personalized products

If you sell things like monogrammed napkins or engraved jewelry, this part matters as much as the fees.

Etsy has personalization built into its listings, so buyers can type in a name or a date when they order.

Squarespace can collect that kind of detail too, with a form that pops up when the customer adds the product to their cart. What it can't do by itself is charge for it. If a monogram costs $10 more, or you charge by the letter, there's no built-in way to add that to the price.

That gap is why I built OptionKit. It adds personalization options with prices to Squarespace product pages, and the total updates before the customer adds to cart. It's $12 a month per store and needs the Core plan or higher. If you're weighing Shopify too, here's my Squarespace vs Shopify comparison, and a closer look at Squarespace vs Shopify for personalized products.

Can you use Squarespace and Etsy together?

Yes, and it's a common setup. Etsy keeps bringing in new shoppers, and your own site is where repeat customers come back to and where you keep more of each sale.

Squarespace helps with the move:

  • You can import your Etsy products into Squarespace with a file, so you don't have to retype every listing.

  • It's a one-time copy, not a sync. Stock is tracked separately in each place, so when something sells on one, you update the other yourself.

  • Squarespace has its own product reviews, and it can show reviews you've imported from Etsy.

Which one should you pick?

  • Start on Etsy if you're new, you don't have an audience yet, and you want to find out whether people will buy.

  • Add Squarespace once you have repeat customers, a following, or enough sales that Etsy's fees are adding up.

  • Go Squarespace only if your customers already find you somewhere else, like Instagram or local markets, and you don't need Etsy's search.

Frequently asked questions

Is Squarespace cheaper than Etsy?

It depends on how much you sell. Etsy has no monthly fee but takes about 10% of each sale. Squarespace has a monthly plan and takes about 3.5%. With $50 orders, Squarespace's Core plan costs less once you pass about nine sales a month.

Can I connect my Etsy shop to Squarespace?

You can import your Etsy products into Squarespace with a file. It's a one-time copy, not a live connection, so stock and orders are tracked separately in each place.

Does Squarespace charge listing fees?

No. Squarespace doesn't charge per listing, and every plan lets you sell an unlimited number of products.

Should I leave Etsy for my own website?

You don't have to pick one. You can keep Etsy for new shoppers who find you through its search, and send your repeat customers to your own site.

Conclusion

Etsy is the easier place to start, and Squarespace is the better place to grow. You don't have to choose one forever. You can keep both, and move more of your sales to your own site as your customers get to know you.

title: How to Set Up Sales Tax on a Squarespace Store
excerpt: Does Squarespace collect sales tax? Yes, once you set it up. Automated vs manual taxes, step-by-step setup, what it costs, and what's still on you.
seoTitle: Squarespace Sales Tax: How to Set It Up (Automated or Manual)
seoDescription: Does Squarespace collect sales tax? Yes, once you set it up. Automated vs manual taxes, step-by-step setup, what it costs, and what's still on you.
imageAlt: Two ways to set up sales tax in Squarespace: automated or manual
body:
Note: I'm a web designer, not a tax advisor. This post covers how the tax settings in Squarespace work, as of November 25, 2026. For what your business owes and where, talk to an accountant or your state's tax office.

Sales tax is the setting most store owners are nervous about getting wrong. The good news is that the Squarespace part is pretty simple. The harder part is knowing where you need to collect, and that isn't a Squarespace question.

Here's what Squarespace does, what it leaves to you, and how to set it up either way.

Does Squarespace collect sales tax?

Yes. Once you set up tax rates, Squarespace works out the tax at checkout and adds it to the customer's order. The money lands in your account with the rest of the sale.

It doesn't collect anything until you set it up, though. A brand new store charges no tax.

Does Squarespace remit sales tax for you?

No. Squarespace collects the tax from your customer and passes it to you. Registering with your state, filing returns and paying what you collected are all still your job.

On your own Squarespace site, you're the seller, so the paperwork is yours.

Automated or manual: which one should you use?

Squarespace gives you two ways to set up tax, and you pick one. You can't use both.

AutomatedManual
How rates are setYou pick where you're registered, and Squarespace works out the rateYou type in each rate
PlansCore, Plus and AdvancedEvery plan
CostA small fee per order, capped at $0.99No extra fee
Different rates for different productsYes, with product tax codesNo
Tax holidaysApplied for youNot applied for you

The automated fee depends on your plan: 0.15% of the order on Core, 0.10% on Plus and 0.05% on Advanced. On a $100 order on Core, that's 15 cents.

My take: if you only collect tax in one state and everything you sell is taxed the same way, manual is fine. If you're registered in more than one state, or you sell things that are taxed differently, like clothing or food, automated is worth the few cents.

How to set up automated sales tax on Squarespace

  1. If you've added tax settings in PayPal or another payment account, remove them so tax isn't charged twice. If you use TaxJar, disconnect it.

  2. Open the Taxes panel. It's under Settings, or press / and search for "Taxes."

  3. Click Automated and add your business details.

  4. Add your Tax address. This is your main business address.

  5. Pick a default Product tax code. This tells Squarespace what kind of thing you sell.

  6. Click Add Registrations and select the states where you're registered to collect tax.

  7. Save. When you see a green Collecting status, it's working.

Only add the states where you're actually registered.

How to add sales tax manually

  1. Open the Taxes panel.

  2. Under Manual Setup, click Add Rate.

  3. Choose United States, then select your state. There's no single rate for the whole country, so you add one state at a time.

  4. Enter the state's rate.

  5. If your state taxes shipping, turn on Charge taxes on shipping. If it taxes services and downloads, turn on Charge taxes on services and digital products.

  6. Save.

If your city or county adds its own tax, you can add a rate for one ZIP code or a range of ZIP codes. Squarespace adds it on top of the state rate.

A few things that surprise people

  • Which address counts. Physical products are taxed by where they ship. Downloads and services are taxed by the billing address.

  • Local pickup. Pickup orders use the customer's billing address unless you add a taxation address to the pickup option. Add your shop's address so pickups are taxed at your local rate.

  • Discounts. Tax is worked out on the price after the discount.

  • Gift cards. Buying a gift card isn't taxed. The tax is charged later, when someone spends it.

  • Tax-exempt customers. With manual rates, there's no way to mark one customer as exempt.

  • Prices with tax included. If you'd rather show one price with tax already in it, choose Include in price in the Taxes panel.

Which plan do you need?

Manual tax rates work on every plan that can sell, including Basic. Automated taxes need Core or higher. If you're on Basic and thinking about moving up, I go through what each plan costs in my Squarespace pricing post.

Frequently asked questions

Does Squarespace collect sales tax automatically?

It can. On the Core, Plus and Advanced plans, you can turn on automated taxes, and Squarespace works out the rate for each order in the states where you're registered. On the Basic plan, you add the rates yourself.

Does Squarespace file or pay my sales tax?

No. Squarespace collects the tax at checkout and it comes to you with the rest of the sale. Registering, filing and paying are up to you.

How much does automated sales tax cost on Squarespace?

There's a fee on each order: 0.15% on Core, 0.10% on Plus and 0.05% on Advanced, capped at $0.99 per order. Manual tax rates have no extra fee.

Can I charge sales tax on shipping in Squarespace?

Yes. With manual rates, turn on Charge taxes on shipping for each state where shipping is taxed.

Can I still use TaxJar with Squarespace?

Not together with automated taxes. Squarespace's automated taxes replace TaxJar, and you have to disconnect TaxJar before you turn them on.

Conclusion

Setting up sales tax in Squarespace takes a few minutes once you know where you need to collect. Sort that part out first with your state or an accountant. Then pick automated or manual, place a test order, and check that the tax line looks right.

title: The Right Squarespace Image Size for Product Photos
excerpt: The best image size for Squarespace is 2500 pixels wide and under 500 KB. Here's why, plus the right shape, file type and settings for product photos.
seoTitle: Squarespace Image Size: The Right Size for Product Photos
seoDescription: The best image size for Squarespace is 2500 pixels wide and under 500 KB. Here's why, plus the right shape, file type and settings for product photos.
imageAlt: Squarespace image size guide: 2500 pixels wide, under 500 KB, JPG for photos, RGB color
body:
If your product photos look blurry, load slowly or get cropped in odd places, it usually comes down to the files you uploaded. Squarespace is forgiving about image size, but a few numbers make a real difference.

Here's the short version, then the reasons behind it.

What is the best image size for Squarespace?

  • Width: 2500 pixels. Don't go under 1500.

  • File size: 500 KB or less if you can. The limit is 20 MB.

  • File type: JPG for photos. PNG for images with a see-through background or text in them.

  • Color: RGB, with an sRGB profile.

  • Shape: the same for every product photo.

These are Squarespace's own recommendations, and they apply to product photos and to most other images on your site.

Why 2500 pixels wide?

When you upload an image, Squarespace makes up to seven copies of it at different widths, from 100 pixels up to 2500. Then it shows each visitor the copy that fits their screen. A phone gets a small one, and a big monitor gets a big one.

If you upload at 2500 pixels wide, Squarespace has everything it needs to make all seven. If your image is narrower than 1500 pixels, the bigger copies don't exist, and the photo can look blurry on a computer screen even though it looks fine on your phone.

You don't need to go wider than 2500. It won't look any sharper, and the upload takes longer.

What about DPI?

You can ignore it. DPI only matters for printing. On a screen, the pixel width is what counts, so a 72 DPI image and a 300 DPI image with the same pixel width look the same on your site.

What shape should product images be?

Squarespace doesn't require a certain shape. What matters is that all your product photos are the same shape, so your store page lines up in a tidy grid.

Square (1:1) is the safe choice, and it's what I'd pick for most stores. A tall 2:3 or 4:5 shape works well for clothing and anything else that's taller than it is wide.

Pick one, and crop your photos to it before you upload. If you let Squarespace do the cropping, it can cut off the top or the sides of a product.

To set the shape your store page uses in Squarespace 7.1:

  1. Edit your store page and hover over the section with your products.

  2. Click the pencil icon.

  3. Choose the aspect ratio. This is also where you set the spacing and the number of columns.

The setting applies to every product on that page. So if your photos are 4:5 and the page is set to square, they'll all be cropped.

How to keep image files small

Big image files are a common reason a store page loads slowly. Squarespace recommends keeping each image at 500 KB or less, and keeping a whole page under 5 MB.

  • Resize first. A photo straight off a phone or camera is often 4000 pixels wide or more. Bring it down to 2500.

  • Save photos as JPG. A PNG of the same photo can be several times bigger.

  • Turn the quality down a little. Around 80% is usually plenty, and most people can't see the difference.

Squarespace also converts your images to a faster format called WebP when it shows them to visitors. You don't have to do anything for that.

How many images can a product have?

Up to 100, but you don't want anywhere near that many. Four to six good photos is plenty for most products.

The first image in the product editor is the featured image by default. That's the one that shows on your store page, so make it your clearest shot of the product.

If a product comes in different colors, you can add an image to each variant. When a customer picks "Blue," they see the blue one.

File names and alt text

  • File names: use letters, numbers and hyphens, like brass-compass-open.jpg. Accents and symbols like & or % can cause upload problems.

  • Alt text: a short description of what's in the photo. It helps people who use screen readers, and it helps your photos show up in Google Images. Each product image can have up to 200 characters.

To add alt text, open the product editor and click Images. Click ••• on the image, then Edit Metadata.

What about banner images?

Banners at the top of a page are a different case. They don't have a set shape, because they stretch to fit whatever screen they're on. Use the same 2500 pixel width, and keep the important part of the photo near the middle, since the edges can get cropped on smaller screens.

When photos aren't enough

Photos do a lot of the selling on a product page, and reviews do much of the rest. If you haven't turned those on, here's how to add product reviews to Squarespace.

Good photos show what the product looks like. They can't show a customer what they can change about it, like the thread color on a monogram or the font for an engraving. For that you need options on the product page. Here's my guide to adding product options in Squarespace, starting with what the built-in tools can do.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best image size for Squarespace?

2500 pixels wide, and 500 KB or less if you can. Images narrower than 1500 pixels can look blurry on a computer screen.

What size should Squarespace product images be?

2500 pixels wide, with every product photo the same shape. Square (2500 by 2500) is the safe choice. Squarespace doesn't require exact dimensions.

What is the maximum image size on Squarespace?

20 MB per image. For a fast site, Squarespace recommends 500 KB or less.

Does DPI matter for Squarespace images?

No. DPI only affects printing. On a website, the pixel width is what matters.

Should I use JPG or PNG on Squarespace?

JPG for photos, because the files are much smaller. PNG for logos, images with a see-through background and images with text in them.

Conclusion

You don't need exact dimensions for Squarespace. You need photos that are 2500 pixels wide, small in file size, and all the same shape. Get those three right and most blurry, slow or badly cropped images fix themselves.

title: How to Take Pre-Orders on Squarespace
excerpt: Squarespace has no pre-order button, but there are two ways to take pre-orders: a pre-order product that takes payment now, or a waitlist.
seoTitle: Squarespace Pre-Orders: How to Set Them Up (2 Ways)
seoDescription: Squarespace has no pre-order button, but there are two ways to take pre-orders: a pre-order product that takes payment now, or a waitlist.
imageAlt: Two ways to take pre-orders on Squarespace: a pre-order product that takes payment now, or a waitlist with no payment yet
body:
Squarespace doesn't have a pre-order button you can switch on. That surprises people, because pre-orders are such a common way to launch a product or find out how many to make.

You can still take pre-orders on Squarespace. There are two ways to do it, and which one you want depends on whether you'd like the money now or later.

Can you take pre-orders on Squarespace?

Yes. Squarespace's own help center says there's no dedicated pre-order feature, and suggests two ways to do it instead:

  • A pre-order product. A normal product with the button changed to "Pre-order." Customers pay now, and you ship when it's ready.

  • A waitlist. Customers leave their email and get a message when the product is in stock. Nobody pays until then.

Way 1: Set up a pre-order product

This works on every Squarespace plan that can sell.

  1. Add the product the way you'd add any other product.

  2. Set the stock above zero, so it doesn't show as sold out. If you're only making 50, set it to 50. If you're using pre-orders to see how many to make, set it high.

  3. In the description, say clearly when it will ship. "Ships the week of March 2" is better than "Ships in spring."

  4. In the product editor, go to Details, type Pre-order in the Button text field, and click Save.

Orders come in like any other order. When the product arrives, you fulfill them from the Orders panel.

A few things make this go more smoothly:

  • Put "pre-order" in the product name too. Not everyone reads the description, and the button text is easy to miss.

  • Link your store policies. Say what happens if the date slips, and whether someone can cancel.

  • Think about mixed orders. If someone buys a pre-order item with something that's in stock, decide whether you'll ship twice or hold the order, and say so on the page. Your shipping options apply to pre-orders like any other order.

  • Change the button back. Once the product is in stock, set the button text to "Add to cart" again and update the description.

Way 2: Use a waitlist

A waitlist is the lower-risk option. You're not holding anyone's money, so a late shipment doesn't turn into refund requests.

  1. Open the Waitlists panel. You can press / and search for it.

  2. Open the panel's settings and turn on Allow Waitlist Signups.

  3. Set the product's stock to zero.

Now the sold-out product page shows a box where shoppers can leave their email. When you add stock, open the waitlist, click the product, and click Email all.

What to know before you count on it:

  • Waitlists are on the Core, Plus and Advanced plans, not Basic. Here's what each plan costs.

  • They work for physical products and services.

  • They're all or nothing. When waitlists are on, every sold-out product gets one.

  • The signup box doesn't show if your variants display as buttons. Use a dropdown.

  • You can see the list, but you can't export it.

Which one should you use?

Pre-order productWaitlist
Customer paysNowWhen it's in stock
PlansEvery plan that can sellCore and higher
Tells you how many to makeYes, in real ordersRoughly, in signups
If your date slipsYou may owe refundsNothing to refund

If you need the money to pay for the production run, use a pre-order product. If you only want to know who's interested, a waitlist is simpler.

Can you take a deposit instead of the full price?

Not automatically. Squarespace charges the full product price at checkout. One way around it is to sell the deposit as its own product, priced at the deposit amount, and send an invoice for the rest when the item is ready. Say on the page what the full price is and when the rest is due, so nobody's surprised.

Pre-orders for made-to-order products

Some pre-orders are really made-to-order: the customer picks a size, a color or a name to be printed, and you make it after they pay. Squarespace handles sizes and colors with variants. For choices that change the price, like adding a name for $8, you'll need a product option with a price. Here's my guide to adding product options in Squarespace, which covers the built-in tools and the plugin I built for the rest.

Frequently asked questions

Does Squarespace have a pre-order feature?

Not a dedicated one. You set up a normal product, change the button text to Pre-order and say when it ships. Or you turn on waitlists and email shoppers when it's in stock.

imageAlt: How a review gets on a Squarespace product page: you fulfill the order, Squarespace emails the customer, they leave a review
body:
Product reviews are built into Squarespace, but they're off until you turn them on, and the setting isn't where most people look for it. It isn't in your store settings. It's an automated email.

Here's how Squarespace product reviews work, how to turn them on, and what they can't do.

How do product reviews work on Squarespace?

Squarespace reviews come from customers who bought something. Squarespace asks them for you, by email:

  1. A customer buys something and you mark the order fulfilled.

  2. 14 days later, Squarespace emails them and asks for a review.

  3. They give each item 1 to 5 stars and can write up to 1,500 characters.

  4. The review shows at the bottom of that product's page.

Customers have 120 days from their purchase to leave a review. An order with several products gets one email, and the customer can review each product in it.

Which plans have product reviews?

Review request emails are on all four current plans: Basic, Core, Plus and Advanced. You don't need to upgrade for this one.

Customers can review physical products, downloads, services and subscriptions. Gift cards can't be reviewed.

How to add product reviews to Squarespace

  1. Open your automations dashboard. The quickest way is to press / and search for "Automations."

  2. Click Request customer reviews.

  3. To change the email, click Action, then Edit Email. You can change the wording, the subject line, the colors and the fonts.

  4. Click Send Test to see it in your own inbox.

  5. Click Go live.

From then on, every fulfilled order gets a review request. Orders you fulfilled in the 14 days before you turned it on get one too.

Keep the email short. A line of thanks and a clear button is enough. People are doing you a favor, so make it quick for them.

How to show reviews on your product pages

Once your first review comes in, open the Customer Reviews panel and go to its settings. You have three choices for what shows on a product page:

  • Product reviews only. Reviews for the product the customer is looking at.

  • Store reviews only. Every review from your whole store, on every product page.

  • Product and store reviews. Both, in two tabs.

If you're just starting out, I'd choose store reviews. Five reviews spread across your shop look better on every page than one product with five and the rest with none. Switch to product reviews once most of your products have a few.

Make sure the Requested reviews toggle is on, or reviews won't show on your product pages at all. The same settings have a toggle to email you whenever a new review comes in. Turn that on too.

If you also sell on Etsy, Squarespace can show reviews you've imported from there. They appear with your store reviews, not under individual products. I compare the two in Squarespace vs Etsy.

What Squarespace reviews can't do

  • You can't reply to a review. If you want to respond, you email the customer.

  • You can't delete a review. You can hide one, which also takes it out of your average rating.

  • Customers can't edit a review after they send it.

  • You can't send the request again. Each order gets one email. You also can't change the 14 days.

  • In-person sales don't count. Orders taken through point of sale don't get a review request.

  • You can't export reviews or move them to another site.

  • The stars are always black. You can't change their color in the settings.

Why aren't my customers getting the review email?

Check these in order:

  • Has it been 14 days? The clock starts when you fulfill the order, not when it's placed.

  • Is the order marked fulfilled? Unfulfilled orders never get a request.

  • Is the automation live? It pauses by itself while you're editing the email.

  • Is it in their spam folder? Automated emails end up there sometimes.

Do you need a reviews plugin?

For most small stores, no. The built-in reviews cover the basics, they're included in your plan, and they come from people who really bought from you.

You'd look at a separate review tool if you need something the built-in ones can't do, like replying to a review in public. That's true of Squarespace in general: it covers the basics well, and plugins fill in the gaps. I keep a list of the ones I've made on my free Squarespace plugins page.

Frequently asked questions

Yes. Product reviews are built in on the Basic, Core, Plus and Advanced plans. You turn them on by setting the Request customer reviews automation live.

When does Squarespace send the review request email?

14 days after you mark the order fulfilled. You can't change the timing, and each order gets one email.

Can I delete a bad review on Squarespace?

You can't delete a review, but you can hide it. Hiding a review also removes it from your average rating.

Can I reply to a review on Squarespace?

No. There's no public reply. To respond, email the customer.

Can I import my Etsy reviews into Squarespace?

Squarespace can show reviews imported from Etsy. They appear with your store reviews, not under individual products.

Conclusion

Turning on reviews takes a few minutes, and then it runs without you. Set the automation live, choose store reviews while you're building up, and make sure you mark orders fulfilled so the emails go out.

seoDescription: After years of telling clients "Squarespace can't do that," my studio built OptionKit: engraving, gift wrap, custom text and photo uploads, with prices.
body:
I have a confession.

For years, there was one question from clients that I dreaded:

"Can customers add engraving for $15?"

Or gift wrap for $5. Or a name on a cake. Or a photo on a mug.

And every time, I had to say some version of: "Squarespace can't really do that. We can fake it with variants... or you could move to Shopify."

I hated that answer. I move people TO Squarespace so they can run their own website without calling a developer. Telling them to leave over one missing feature felt wrong.

The last straw was a client with a small shop who wanted customers to type a name for engraving and pay a little extra for it. I spent an afternoon trying every workaround I knew. At the end of it I thought: why doesn't this just exist?

So my studio built the thing I kept wishing existed. It's called OptionKit, and it's out now.

What Is OptionKit?

OptionKit is a plugin that adds product options with prices to Squarespace stores.

Your customer picks what they want on the product page. The price updates as they go. And then they pay for all of it in your normal Squarespace cart and checkout.

It lives under a new sister brand to Clementine called JuiceKit. (Yes, we stuck with the fruit theme. 🍊)

What Can You Add to a Product?

There are seven kinds of options, and you can mix them on one product:

  • Text field: "Name to engrave." Free, a set price, or priced per letter.

  • Text box: A longer gift message or special instructions.

  • Checkbox: "Add laser engraving, +$15."

  • Dropdown, buttons, or color swatches: "Frame: Oak, Walnut, Black." Each choice can have its own price.

  • Quantity: "Extra candles, $0.75 each."

  • File upload: A photo, a logo, or a design file sent with the order.

  • Info text: A note between options, like "Made to order: ships in 2 weeks."

And a few things that make it feel polished:

  • Options can show only when they apply. The font choice only appears after "Add engraving" is checked.

  • You can set limits, so nobody orders a 90-letter engraving.

  • It matches your site. Options use your template's fonts and colors, on phones and computers.

How Does It Charge for Options?

This is the clever part, so stick with me.

Squarespace can only charge for products. So each option with a price becomes a small product in your store, like "Laser engraving, $15," on a page that isn't in your menu. OptionKit creates those for you.

When a customer adds a cutting board with engraving, OptionKit adds the engraving to the cart in the same click.

Squarespace does the rest - the cart, discount codes, taxes, checkout, the order, the email. Nothing about your checkout changes.

On the order, you see exactly what each customer chose, right next to the item it belongs to. So two boards with two different names stay two clear jobs.

Who Is It For?

Anyone on Squarespace 7.1 who sells something customers personalize:

  • Engravers and woodworkers (see the engraving setup)

  • Bakeries (custom cakes)

  • Florists (flowers)

  • Framers and print shops (framing)

  • Embroiderers (monograms)

How Long Does Setup Take?

About half an hour. There's no code to write.

  1. Build your options. Start from a template like Engraving or Custom cake, with a preview right next to it.

  2. Connect your store. Paste one line into Squarespace's Code Injection, once.

  3. Publish. Your options are on your store in about a minute.

After that, every change is one click. Nothing to paste again.

What Does It Cost?

  • Free on your site's squarespace.com address, for as long as you like. Build and test everything.

  • Free for 14 days on your own domain, with no card.

  • Then $12 a month or $120 a year per store.

There are no per-order fees and no limits on products or options. One $15 engraving pays for the month.

What It Doesn't Do (Yet)

I'd rather be upfront:

  • It's for Squarespace 7.1. It doesn't work on 7.0.

  • You need a plan with Code Injection. That's Core, Plus, or Advanced, or an older Business or Commerce plan.

  • No live preview on the product photo yet. Customers see their choices and the price update, but they don't see their text on the photo. That's coming soon.

Try It

The fastest way to understand it is to play with it. Try the live demo store here - check a box, type a name, upload a photo, and watch the price change.

Then try OptionKit free on your own store.

Final Thoughts

I built this because I needed it for my own clients. Now, when someone asks "can customers add engraving for $15?", I finally get to say yes.

If you'd like OptionKit set up for you, or you want a whole store designed around it, book a free consultation. I'd love to see what you're selling.

From what I've seen, most people care more about whether your photo looks professional and actually looks like you than how it was made. An AI photo can hurt you if you show up to an interview looking very different from your picture, or if the photo has obvious AI mistakes like blurry eyes or strange lighting. Pick one that looks natural and looks like you.

How much do AI headshot generators cost?

Most paid AI headshot generators cost somewhere between $15 and $40, and you usually get anywhere from 40 to 100+ photos with different outfits, poses and backgrounds. A local photographer usually charges $200 to $500 or more for a basic studio session, so AI is a much cheaper option.

Is there a good free AI headshot generator?

There are more free options now, including tools from Canva and Adobe, and Profile Pic Maker has a free tier. I haven't tested the free ones with my own photos yet, so I can't tell you how they compare. If you just need a quick placeholder, they could be worth a try. For a LinkedIn photo that really looks like you, PhotoPacks.AI is what I'd use.

Do AI headshots look fake?

They definitely can. As you saw above, the cheaper generators gave me the wrong eye color, waxy skin and outlines around my face. The better tools have gotten a lot more realistic, and my best PhotoPacks.AI photos looked like real photos of me.

How many photos do I need to upload for AI headshots?

It depends on the tool. PhotoPacks.AI asks for 10, and ProfilePicture.AI wanted at least 20 when I tested it. A good mix helps: close-ups, chest-up shots, different angles and different lighting. Skip group photos, heavy filters, and photos where sunglasses or a hat cover your face.

Which AI generator is best for people with glasses?

AI often has trouble with glasses. It can warp the frames or add glare that hides your eyes. In my test, PhotoPacks.AI handled glasses the best. The frames kept their shape and my eyes looked normal behind the lenses.

Tip: include several photos of yourself wearing your glasses from different angles, so the AI can see how they sit on your face.

Can I use AI headshots on my Squarespace website?

Yes, but check the size. Squarespace recommends images between 1500 and 2500 pixels wide, and small 512px files will look blurry on a computer screen. PhotoPacks.AI gives you high-resolution images, which work well on a website. If you want a wide banner, you can use Canva or Photoshop to extend the background, or pick a headshot with a plain background that's easy to crop.

Is your website holding you hostage?

It’s a specific kind of panic. You need to update your pricing or change a team member's photo, but you stare at your dashboard and freeze. You're scared that if you click the wrong button, the whole site breaks.

They tell me, “Mali, it’s too complicated. I’m scared to touch it.”

My design philosophy is simple: No one should be held hostage by their website platform.

Here is why migrating from WordPress to Squarespace is the best business move you can make in 2026, and why I refuse to build sites that require a developer to maintain.

1. The Hidden Cost of WordPress Maintenance

When you hired your original designer, they probably told you WordPress was the "professional" choice. They didn't mention the upkeep.

To keep a WordPress site secure, you (or a hired pro) need to:

  • Update plugins weekly (and fix them when they break your layout).

  • Run security backups so you don't get hacked.

  • Pay for managed hosting fees.

I’ve had clients paying a high hourly rate to developers just for basic "maintenance" tasks. That’s money that should be going into your marketing, not keeping the lights on.

When we migrate your site to Squarespace, that maintenance budget drops to $0.

Squarespace handles all the security, updates, and hosting in the background. You never have to pay me to "update a plugin" again.

2. "Can I Edit My Own Website?" (Yes, Finally)

This is the main reason I move therapists, law firms, and small business owners to Squarespace.

On WordPress, the dashboard looks like the cockpit of an alien spaceship. On Squarespace, the dashboard looks like... a drag-and-drop canvas.

In many cases, my clients see their rankings go UP after switching because the new site is faster, mobile-friendly, and easier for Google to read.

Final Thoughts: Take Back Control

You shouldn't have to wait a week to post a new service. You shouldn't have to pay a "ransom" in hourly fees just to keep your website online.

title: The Hidden Costs of Squarespace: A 2026 Pricing Breakdown (Transaction Fees, Email & Scheduling)
excerpt: Does Squarespace take a cut of your sales? How much is Acuity really? As a Squarespace expert, I see clients get confused by these fees constantly. I’m breaking down the real cost of running a site in 2026 so you can budget with confidence.
seoTitle: Squarespace Pricing Guide 2026: Hidden Fees, Transaction Costs & Add-Ons
seoDescription: Confused by Squarespace fees? I break down the real cost of Squarespace Payments, transaction fees, Acuity Scheduling, and Member Areas in this 2026 guide.
body:
Note: All prices listed below are for the US and were last checked on November 25, 2026, after Squarespace raised its prices in July 2026. Pricing changes often, so I’ve included links to the official pages so you can always check the live rates.

Let’s be real: Trying to figure out the actual price of a Squarespace website can feel like a scavenger hunt.

You look at the main pricing page and see a base monthly fee. You think, "Okay, $29/month. That fits my budget."

But that base price is just the starting line.

Once you actually start building your business, the costs begin to layer on. You realize that selling a product triggers a transaction fee. Sending a branded newsletter is an extra subscription. Want to let clients book appointments? That’s another add-on cost.

Suddenly, your $29/month bill looks a lot different.

The problem is that Squarespace lists all these fees on five different support pages, making it nearly impossible to get a clear picture of your total overhead.

I wanted to stop the madness. So, I decided to consolidate it all right here. I’ve pulled the data from the commerce page, the scheduling page, and the email marketing page to bring it all into one easy-to-read guide.

My goal is to make this as simple as possible so you don’t have to have 15 tabs open just to figure out what your website will actually cost.

Here is exactly what you are paying for when you build a Squarespace site in 2026: from the base "rent" to the necessary "utilities" all in one place.

1. The "Rent": Monthly Hosting Fees

First, you have the base cost. This is just to have your website exist on the internet. Currently, Squarespace has 4 main plans: Basic, Core, Plus, and Advanced. Paid yearly, they cost $19, $29, $49 and $99 a month. If you want the full picture, including what it costs to have a site designed, see my post on how much a Squarespace website costs.

  • The Basic Plan is great for portfolios and simple brochures.

  • The Core/Plus/Advanced Plans unlock more features like e-commerce analytics and better merchandising tools.

But the monthly fee is just the start. If you plan to sell anything (services, products, or donations), you need to know about the fees below.

2. The "Hidden" Fees: Getting Paid

This is the part that usually trips people up. There are actually two types of fees that come out of your sales.

A. Credit Card Processing Fees (The Bank's Cut)

No matter what plan you are on, if a client pays you with a credit card, the processor takes a cut. You cannot avoid this (it’s how Visa/Mastercard make money).

You generally have three options for processing payments:

Option 1: Squarespace Payments (The New Standard)

Squarespace recently launched their own processor to compete with Stripe. The fee depends on which hosting plan you are on:

  • Basic Plan: 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction

  • Core Plan: 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction

  • Plus Plan: 2.7% + $0.30 per transaction

  • Advanced Plan: 2.5% + $0.30 per transaction (Best for high volume!)

> Check the most updated Squarespace Transaction Fees here.

Option 2: Stripe

If you stick with the classic Stripe integration, the standard US rate is usually 2.9% + 30¢ per transaction, regardless of your Squarespace plan.
> Check current Stripe Pricing here.

Option 3: PayPal

If you allow clients to pay via PayPal, their fees are slightly different, typically 2.99% + a fixed fee (which varies by country).
> Check current PayPal Business Fees here.

B. The Squarespace "Transaction Fee" (The Platform Cut)

Heads up: This is separate from the credit card fee!

  • If you are on the BASIC Plan: Squarespace takes an additional 2% cut of every sale.

    • My professional advice: The Basic plan is okay for "proof of concept" if you are on a tight budget. But once you start making regular sales, that 2% adds up fast. It’s usually better to upgrade to the Core plan (where this fee drops to 0%) to save money in the long run.

  • If you are on Core, Plus, or Advanced: Squarespace takes 0%. You only pay the credit card processing fee.

3. The Add-Ons: Courses, Scheduling & Email

These features are powerful, but they are not included in your base hosting bill.

Selling Courses (Member Areas)

Want to create a paywall or sell a digital course? Squarespace calls these "Member Areas." Just like the commerce fees, they take a percentage of your course sales depending on your plan:

  • Basic Plan: 7% fee

  • Core Plan: 5% fee

  • Plus Plan: 1% fee

  • Advanced Plan: 0% fee

Again, if you plan to sell a $500 course, do NOT stay on the Basic plan, or you'll be donating 7% of that straight to Squarespace!

Booking Appointments (Acuity Scheduling)

If you are a therapist, coach, or yoga studio, you probably know Acuity Scheduling. Squarespace acquired them a while back. It integrates perfectly, but it requires a separate subscription.

  • Starter Plan (~$16/mo annually): Great for solo business owners.

  • Standard Plan (~$27/mo annually): Adds text message reminders (crucial for reducing no-shows!) and subscriptions/packages.

  • Premium Plan (~$55/mo annually): Needed for HIPAA compliance, multiple time zones, and multiple staff calendars.

> Check the most updated Acuity Pricing here.

Email Campaigns (Newsletters)

You can collect email addresses for free using a Newsletter Block on your site. But if you want to send pretty, branded emails directly from Squarespace, you need an Email Campaigns subscription.

  • The Free Trial: You can send up to 3 blast emails (5,000 sends per email) to test it out. Note: You don't get automated emails on the trial.

  • Paid Plans: Start at roughly $8/mo (annually) for 500 emails/month.

  • Why pay? It allows you to set up automations. For example, if someone downloads your "Free Guide," Squarespace can automatically email it to them. The price scales up based on how many emails you send (up to $118/mo for 500k emails).

> Check the rates at the bottom of the Squarespace Email Pricing page.

Final Thoughts: Don't Let the Math Scare You

I know… it looks like a lot of numbers. But here is the good news: You can start small.

Most of my clients start on the Core Plan (to avoid the 2% transaction fee) and add Acuity or Email Campaigns later as they grow.

The beauty of Squarespace is that everything is in one place. You don't need a separate Mailchimp account, a separate WordPress hosting bill, and a separate Calendly invoice. It’s all under one roof.

Confused about which plan is right for you? You don't have to figure it out alone. Book a free consultation and I’ll help you pick the setup that saves you the most money based on your business goals.
